title: Kernel-aware anticipatory phase splitter for latency-fairness tradeoffs
creator: Maya Brooks
description:
Problem: Current prefill/decode scheduling treats phase splitting heuristics and kernel selection as largely orthogonal. This causes suboptimal tail-latency and tenant unfairness in mixed workloads: kernels chosen at runtime can change per-tenant cost and latency, and static phase split heuristics either over-split (wasting throughput) or under-split (increasing latency for short requests).

Proposal: Implement an anticipatory phase-splitter that uses light-weight kernel-cost probes + sequence-length prediction to decide at request admission time how to split prefill and decode phases and which kernel variant hints to attach. The component combines three parts: (1) a kernel-cost estimator service (cheap probe + history) that predicts per-request kernel latency and memory pressure across candidate kernels; (2) a phase-split decision module that balances latency SLOs and throughput utility using a configurable objective (latency-first vs throughput-first) and tenant weights; (3) a kernel-hint encoder that annotates requests so the runtime scheduler can steer work to the best kernel variant (sparse attention kernels, cached-kv optimized kernels, or fallback dense kernels).

Why different: instead of reacting to delays in decode or globally applying a split, this approach anticipates kernel-level behavior, co-optimizes kernel selection with how many tokens to prefill vs decode, and exposes per-request kernel hints for better downstream routing and batching behavior.

Scope: prototype in runtime v2 control plane + scheduler, microbenchmarks on GPU fleet, small canary in hosted API, integration tests for fairness telemetry and degradation policies.
acceptance_criteria: Median tail latency (p95) for small interactive requests (<=32 tokens) improves by >=8% in canary traffic compared to baseline scheduler
No more than 5% regression in steady-state throughput for large-batch workloads (>=512-token streaming) in the same canary window
Tenant fairness metric (95th percentile slowdown ratio across top-10 tenants) improves or remains stable under mixed synthetic trace replay
Kernel-hinting end-to-end plumbing is present: hints are attached at admission, visible in scheduler logs, and respected by kernel selector in >=90% of probe runs
Implementation includes unit tests, integration tests, a design doc, and a GitHub PR with benchmarks attached
design_notes:
Key design decisions and trade-offs considered:
1) Lightweight probing vs history-only: we found purely history based predictions fail for new model variants and cold-started tenants. A tiny probe (single-token micro-inference on a low-priority lane) amortized across similar requests provides immediate kernel latency signal with negligible cost.
2) Probe frequency and noise: probes are rate-limited per tenant + per model version. We smooth predictions with exponential decay to prevent oscillation when kernels switch.
3) Objective formulation: the phase-splitter supports three modes: latency-first (minimize p95 subject to throughput floor), throughput-first (maximize aggregate tokens/s subject to latency cap), and weighted-fairness (minimize max slowdown ratio with tenant weights). Mode is configurable at pool-level.
4) Kernel hinting granularity: hint is a categorical tag (e.g., sparse-attn-v2, kv-optimized, dense-fallback) rather than specific kernel id to keep scheduler portability across hardware families. Kernel selector maps tags to implementations per-node.
5) Safety fallback: if kernel selector does not support hinted variant or probe indicates high memory pressure, the runtime falls back to stable dense path and logs a metric for auto-tuning.
6) Observability: add per-request fields (hint, predicted-latency-ms, probe-latency-ms, split-decision, objective-mode) to request traces and cost/latency dashboards.
implementation_plan: Week 1: Implement kernel-cost probe endpoint and in-memory estimator; add lightweight backing stores for recent probes
Week 2: Implement phase-split decision module with configurable objective and per-tenant weight support
Week 3: Add kernel-hint annotation to admission path and plumb to scheduler; wire logs and traces
Week 4: Microbenchmarks: run offline trace replay (prod traces anonymized) and kernel microbench harness across 4 node types (A100, H100, L40S, V100)
Week 5: Internal canary: 5% of hosted API traffic with latency-first objective; collect metrics for 48h
Week 6: Evaluate canary, iterate on smoothing/thresholds; run throughput regression tests; prepare PR and design doc updates
Week 7: Roll forward to 25% if metrics stable; draft runbook for rollbacks and failure modes
experiments: A: No-split baseline vs static split vs anticipatory-split under mixed workload replay
B: Kernel-hint respected vs ignored to measure scheduling benefits of hint plumbing (measures batch composition changes and kernel choice distribution)
C: Probe rate variations (0.1/sec, 0.5/sec, 1/sec per tenant) to measure signal/noise trade-offs
D: Objective mode comparison (latency-first / throughput-first / weighted-fairness) using synthetic tenant weights to simulate enterprise vs PLG mixes
E: Stress test with kernel eviction/fallback: induce memory pressure to ensure safe fallbacks and correct telemetry
metrics: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency per model and per-tenant
kernel-select distribution (categorical) and success-rate of hints
tenant slowdown ratio (time_per_request seen vs baseline queuing-free time)
fallback-rate (fraction of hinted requests that had to use dense fallback)
throughput-regression % compared to baseline under controlled load
